text: Compressed air is one of the most expensive utilities in the plant. Most of the electricity that goes in comes out as heat.
Here's how a screw compressor works, and how to keep it efficient.
The screw air compressor.
Inside the air end, two rotors mesh: a male rotor with four lobes, and a female rotor with six flutes.
The motor drives the male rotor, and it turns the female rotor on a thin film of oil, with no metal contact between them.
Air is drawn in through a filter and an inlet valve, and trapped in the pockets between the lobes.
As the rotors turn, each pocket moves along and shrinks, until it opens to the outlet at full pressure, typically seven to ten bar.
Squeezing air makes it hot. Without help, it would leave at well over two hundred degrees.
So oil is injected straight into the compression chamber. It seals the gaps between the rotors, lubricates the bearings, and soaks up the heat.
Oil and air leave together, at around eighty to ninety degrees, into the separator tank.
There, the mixture spins, and most of the oil drops out. A fine separator element catches the remaining mist.
A minimum pressure valve holds pressure in the tank, so the oil keeps circulating, and the air moves on to the aftercooler.
The oil flows back through a cooler, a thermostatic valve and a filter. The thermostat keeps the oil warm enough that water never condenses in it.
The aftercooler cools the air, and the water that condenses out is drained away, before the dryer and filters downstream.
About ninety percent of the power that goes in comes out as heat. And every extra bar of pressure costs roughly seven percent more energy.
And that's where the money leaks.
A clogged intake filter starves the air end, so output falls.
Dirty coolers can't shed the heat. The discharge temperature climbs, until the machine trips.
Old oil breaks down and leaves varnish. A tired separator lets oil carry over into the air lines, and clogs, so the pressure drop across it rises.
A stuck thermostat lets the oil run cold and fill with water, or run hot and cook.
And leaks in the air network, often a fifth or more of everything the compressor makes, keep it running for air nobody uses.
Warning signs: a discharge temperature above its normal band.
A rising pressure drop across the separator or the filters.
Oil in the condensate, or downstream, and oil consumption going up.
And the compressor loading more, while production hasn't changed.
So: check temperatures, pressures and drains every day.
Change the intake and oil filters on running hours, or on pressure drop.
Change the oil and the separator on schedule, and use oil analysis to set the interval.
Clean the coolers, and keep the compressor room cool and well ventilated.
Check that the inlet valve unloads cleanly when demand drops, and that belts or couplings are in good shape.
And hunt leaks with an ultrasonic detector, and set the pressure no higher than you really need.
Less pressure. Less power.
